after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & ∗ \\ b & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{a}{b}.$
after.worked_solution:
From the Jordan matrix $J,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=3.
$$

As a result, the first column of $P$ corresponds to an eigenvector of the eigenvalue $\lambda =3.$ 

Now, computing $A-3I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]-(3)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{-1}{1}=-1.$

content.knowledge_point: Finding Elements of a Jordan Canonical Decomposition for a 2x2 Matrix: The Second Column Case
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -12 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-2 & a \\ 1 & b\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ find the value of $3a+6b.$
content.worked_solution:
From the Jordan matrix $J,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=3.
$$

As a result, we obtain that 

- the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ of the eigenvalue $\lambda =3,$

- the second column of $P$ corresponds to the vector ${v}_{2}$ such that $(A-3I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}.$

Now, computing $A-3I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -12 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}]-(3)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -12 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix equation $(A-3I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -12 & -2 \\ 3 & 6 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & -12 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{3}-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get  

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{3} \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $3a+6b=3\cdot (-\frac{5}{3})+6\cdot 1=1.$

after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,y=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,z=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 10\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that the Jordan matrix $J$ consists of one Jordan block $J={J}_{2}(-1).$ 

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(-1) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A-(-1)I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-(-1)I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the second column of $P$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to $\lambda =-1.$ 

Now, computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ -4 & 1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Among the given vectors, only $y$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2,$ since

$$
(A-(-1)I)y=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=x,
$$

and, therefore,

$$
(A-(-1)I)^{2}y=(A-(-1)I)x=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -4 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

and we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\overset{A-(-1)I\,}{\to }[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\overset{A-(-1)I\,}{\to }0.\end{aligned}
$$

The other vectors do not satisfy this condition.
